summary: Reconsulted six saved scholarly references and the Gita, and added Aristotle. Reuse is individually justified; earlier All-books notes remain unchanged.
next: Expand beyond reference encyclopedias into expert interviews, critical reviews, independent essays and reader discussions.

sources.title: Plato
sources.note: The entry connects Plato's continuing influence to open-ended dialogue and distinguishes Plato's authored arguments from testimony about the historical Socrates.

targets.B: Interpretation and dialogue-form evidence for Republic and related texts.
targets.P: Supports Plato's influence and cautions against conflating his voice with Socrates.

sources.limits: A scholarly interpretation, not a comparative world ranking; shorter dialogues require books-only eligibility review.

sources.title: Aristotle
sources.note: The surviving corpus spans logic, biology, metaphysics and ethics. Its frequently unfinished, technical prose differs from lost public writings; later editorial arrangement complicates work identity.

targets.A: Adds scientific and philosophical treatises to the all-subject candidate pool.
targets.N: Supplies early scientific and ethical nonfiction candidates with textual-history cautions.
targets.B: Identifies philosophical treatises and explains reading and editorial difficulties.
targets.P: Documents Aristotle's disciplinary range and long reception.

sources.location: Introduction and section 2, corpus and divisions
sources.limits: Western reception framing; scholarly influence does not establish modern scientific accuracy.

sources.title: Confucius
sources.note: The Analects transmits multiple representations of Confucius. The entry treats ritual, virtue and family-state relations while warning that later traditions select different aspects of his legacy.

targets.B: Supports Analects as ethical-political thought with layered transmission.
targets.P: Distinguishes the historical thinker from later appropriations of Confucius.

sources.limits: Authorship and doctrine are historically underdetermined; no single modern label captures all reception.

sources.title: Immanuel Kant
sources.note: The three Critiques connect epistemology, ethics and judgment through autonomy. The introduction describes Kant's enduring influence across modern philosophical fields.
candidates: Critique of the Power of Judgment

targets.N: Identifies major argumentative nonfiction across knowledge, ethics and aesthetics.
targets.B: Maps three distinct works to the critical system; avoid reducing Kant to one book.
targets.P: Supports breadth and reception of Kant's philosophical contribution.

sources.limits: Introductory interpretation only; competing readings and discriminatory views require additional evidence.

sources.title: W.E.B. Du Bois
sources.note: The entry argues that Du Bois made race a central philosophical problem across social, political and aesthetic inquiry. Its structure separates periods around The Souls of Black Folk.

targets.N: Supports a social-critical book crossing sociology, history and philosophy.
targets.B: Establishes philosophical relevance beyond narrowly disciplinary treatises.
targets.P: Documents Du Bois's contribution to philosophy of race.

sources.limits: Opening and named work sections identified; detailed work-level argument assessment remains pending.

sources.title: Mary Wollstonecraft
sources.note: Wollstonecraft's critique links women's condition to wider social relations and consumption. The entry identifies Vindication's feminist significance and a broader influence on travel writing and Romanticism.
candidates: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

targets.N: Adds feminist political nonfiction with literary-cultural reception.
targets.B: Supports moral-political argument in Vindication, beyond an isolated women's-rights slogan.
targets.P: Documents philosophical scope and influence beyond one famous contribution.

sources.limits: Her bibliography includes fiction and pamphlets; these do not all qualify as nonfiction books.

sources.title: Zhuangzi
sources.note: The text combines narrative, humour and criticism of fixed categories. It is an anthology, reduced by Guo Xiang from an earlier collection; attribution of its inner chapters is traditional.

targets.B: Documents philosophical content and anthology/edition identity.
targets.P: Separates attributed thinker, multiple textual strands and later editor Guo Xiang.

sources.limits: Do not assign all 33 chapters to one author or silently classify the hybrid text as modern nonfiction.

sources.title: The Bhagavad Gītā
sources.note: The article analyzes the Gita as moral argument within the Mahabharata and traces its separate reception. Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva wrote commentaries on it.

targets.B: Adds Indian moral philosophy and explicit embedded-versus-standalone work issues.
targets.P: Provides a reception link among Vedanta commentators; does not treat fictional speakers as historical philosophers.

sources.limits: One interpretive account; epic context and modern religious reception complicate genre classification.
